analysis.one_liner: Lets people sue government officials who violate their constitutional rights, even if the law wasn't clear at the time.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee since May 2025 with three sponsors and no committee vote, no floor vote, and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: When a police officer or other government official violates someone's constitutional rights, courts currently let the official off the hook if the right wasn't 'clearly established' by earlier court decisions — a judge-made rule called qualified immunity. This bill would amend the 1871 civil rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) to say that good faith, a reasonable belief the conduct was lawful, and an unclear state of the law are not defenses. People whose rights were violated could actually recover money damages. The bill was introduced in May 2025 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: People who suffer constitutional violations by state and local officials — police misconduct, wrongful arrest, excessive force, improper searches — and their families. Under current law, many of these cases are thrown out before any evidence is heard because the victim cannot point to a prior court decision finding the exact same conduct unconstitutional. Removing that defense would let juries decide the facts, and victims could recover damages even when the official says they acted in good faith.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a provision to the civil rights statute stating that good faith, a belief that the conduct was lawful, and a right that was not 'clearly established' are not defenses in suits filed after enactment [S2].
It applies to pending cases as well, so people whose lawsuits are already in court would benefit [S2].

The bill's findings state that qualified immunity has severely limited plaintiffs' ability to recover damages and that the doctrine has frustrated Congress's original intent in passing the 1871 Ku Klux Klan Act [S2].
Under current law, courts require victims to identify a prior case with nearly identical facts before the case can even proceed to discovery; this bill would remove that threshold by statute [S2].

analysis.who_pays: State and local government officials — most often police officers — and, indirectly, the governments and insurers that pay judgments against them. Officials who violate rights would face personal liability more often, and their legal departments would defend more cases on the merits rather than winning them early on immunity grounds. Cities and counties that indemnify their employees would bear more of the cost of misconduct judgments.

drawbacks.text: Police unions and law enforcement groups argue the change would expose officers to personal lawsuits for split-second decisions, making it harder to recruit and retain officers and making officers hesitant to act in dangerous situations [S2] — the bill text itself records the counterview that the immunity doctrine is a judge-made addition never passed by Congress [S2].
State and local governments would face higher litigation and judgment costs, which ultimately come from local budgets funded by taxpayers [S2].
Removing the 'clearly established' requirement means officials can be sued over conduct whose legality was genuinely uncertain at the time, raising the risk of liability for honest mistakes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real and well-documented problem: courts themselves acknowledge qualified immunity often defeats meritorious civil rights claims. The cost is more lawsuits against officials and higher judgment costs for local governments, and officers would lose protection for good-faith mistakes. Whether that trade is worth it is a genuine policy dispute, but the bill is a targeted fix — it does not eliminate suits against officials, only the specific defenses courts have added that Congress says were never in the 1871 statute.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and has sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no movement since.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey introduced the bill on May 22, 2025, joined by Sen. Warren and Sen. Sanders [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1].
No further action appears in the bill's history — no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote — and the Congress runs through January 3, 2027 [S4].
Only two senators besides the sponsor have signed on, both from the Democratic side [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Government officials who violate constitutional rights, and the police unions and local governments that benefit from qualified immunity as it stands, are better off with the bill stalled. Victims of misconduct remain unable to recover in the many cases where courts find the right was not clearly established.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Officials shielded from lawsuits, and police unions

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ending Qualified Immunity Act and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by Republicans
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: 55 of 55 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 55 Senate Republicans sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the majority sets the Senate's schedule, which did not include it.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters are from the left of the Senate (two Democrats and one Independent); no Republican signed on, and the Republican majority controls the Judiciary Committee and the floor schedule.

industries.note: Officers would lose the qualified immunity defense and could be sued personally for constitutional violations even when the law was unclear. Unions have historically opposed ending immunity on the ground that it exposes officers to personal liability for on-the-job decisions.

industries.industry: State and local governments and their insurers
industries.note: Governments that indemnify employees would pay more misconduct judgments and defend more cases on the merits. Those costs fall on local budgets, though they arise from misconduct that currently goes uncompensated.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has the support of 3 of 100 senators, all from the Democratic side, and no committee action in roughly two months. Similar versions of this bill have been introduced in multiple prior Congresses and never reached a vote. With Republicans controlling the Senate and the Judiciary Committee, the bill is very likely to die at the end of this Congress without a hearing or a vote.
